Name: Peak near Cabeus B
Blurb: Westernmost Artemis region, a high peak beside Cabeus crater.

Name: Haworth
Blurb: Rim terrain next to Haworth, a large permanently shadowed crater.

Name: Malapert Massif
Blurb: A 5 km-high massif facing Earth, a natural spot for direct-to-Earth links.

Name: Mons Mouton Plateau
Blurb: Broad, flat-topped plateau north of Mons Mouton.

Name: Mons Mouton
Source: NASA region map (center read off the map, +/-10 km)
Blurb: One of the tallest mountains on the Moon, about 6 km high.

Name: Nobile Rim 1
Source: NASA region map; LROC NAC_ROI_MTMOUTONLO1_P854S0353 (+/-10 km)
Blurb: Rim of Nobile crater, also VIPER's planned exploration area.

Name: Nobile Rim 2
Blurb: Second Nobile rim region, farther from the pole.

Name: de Gerlache Rim 2
Blurb: Ridge on the rim of de Gerlache crater, close to the pole.

Name: Slater Plain
Source: NASA region map (center read off the map, +/-10 km, VERIFY)
Blurb: Plain on the far side of the pole from Earth.

Name: IM-2 Athena (Mons Mouton)
Blurb: Landed 6 Mar 2025, tipped over in a 20 m crater; operated about a day.

Name: IM-2 intended site
Blurb: Where Athena was aiming, a few hundred metres from where it came to rest.

Name: IM-1 Odysseus (Malapert A)
Blurb: First US landing in 50 years, Feb 2024. It landed tilted but worked for a week.

Name: Griffin-1 (Mons Mouton, provisional)
Source: Mons Mouton feature centre; no published landing point (Oct 2026)
Blurb: Astrobotic Griffin-1, launch NET Nov 2026. Moves to the real point once NASA publishes it.

Name: Chandrayaan-3 Shiv Shakti point
Blurb: India's lander and rover, 23 Aug 2023. Far from the pole, so the Sun rises high.

Name: Chang'e-7 target
Blurb: China's planned polar lander, aiming for a peak on Shackleton's south-east ridge.

Name: Shackleton ridge, point A
Source: Bussey et al. 2010 (Icarus 208), PGDA product 69: published illumination 81 % of a lunar year at (-89.68, 194.0). Those Kaguya-era coordinates land on a slope in the LOLA 5 m DEMs, so the point was moved 593 m to the best-lit peak within 2 km (85.4 % over 2026, 2 m eye).
Blurb: On the ridge that connects Shackleton to de Gerlache: lit most of the year.

Name: Peak near Shackleton, point B
Source: Bussey et al. 2010 (Icarus 208), PGDA product 69: published illumination 82 % of a lunar year at (-89.44, 218.2). Those Kaguya-era coordinates land on a slope in the LOLA 5 m DEMs, so the point was moved 1379 m to the best-lit peak within 2 km (88.4 % over 2026, 2 m eye).
Blurb: A peak of near-eternal light next to Shackleton.

Name: de Gerlache ridge, point C
Source: Bussey et al. 2010 (Icarus 208), PGDA product 69: published illumination 85 % of a lunar year at (-88.71, 291.3). Those Kaguya-era coordinates land on a slope in the LOLA 5 m DEMs, so the point was moved 1292 m to the best-lit peak within 2 km (83.4 % over 2026, 2 m eye).
Blurb: Ridge on de Gerlache's rim, one of the best-lit spots at the pole.

Name: Peak close to Shackleton, point D
Source: Bussey et al. 2010 (Icarus 208), PGDA product 69: published illumination 86 % of a lunar year at (-88.79, 124.5). Those Kaguya-era coordinates land on a slope in the LOLA 5 m DEMs, so the point was moved 753 m to the best-lit peak within 2 km (84.8 % over 2026, 2 m eye).
Blurb: Peak on Shackleton's far side, lit 86 % of the year.

Name: Malapert Mountain M1
Source: Bussey et al. 2010 (Icarus 208), PGDA product 69: published illumination 74 % of a lunar year at (-86.04, 2.7). Those Kaguya-era coordinates land on a slope in the LOLA 5 m DEMs, so the point was moved 1914 m to the best-lit peak within 2 km (80.6 % over 2026, 2 m eye).
Blurb: Summit of Malapert, with Earth almost always in view.

Name: Geographic south pole (validation)
Blurb: The point we check against JPL Horizons. The true pole is inside Shackleton crater.
